prize_parts.citation: For discoveries of the physiology of glucagon-like peptide-1 and its glucose-dependent insulinotropic and appetite-regulating actions, which made incretin-based treatment of diabetes and obesity possible

statement.case_for: My preferred configuration is unchanged: one prize part, B027, to Drucker, Holst and Mojsov. The scientific case did not move in round 1 because nobody contested it. The mechanism is specific (a proglucagon-derived incretin with glucose-dependent insulin secretion, satiety and gastric-emptying actions), it has been independently confirmed for more than two decades, and it now has randomized outcome evidence in diabetes, obesity, and cardiovascular and renal disease. The Medicine prize is for discoveries of benefit to humankind, and few candidates join a physiological core to clinical effect of this scale. The chair's third question asks whether the citation honours the peptide or the whole arc. I would honour the physiology and the active peptide, and the citation says the discoveries made treatment possible. That wording credits the enabling discovery and does not claim the drugs themselves. Holst established human GLP-1 physiology, Drucker established the receptor biology and the therapeutic concept, and Mojsov identified and synthesised the active GLP-1(7-36) peptide, so together they are the discovery that the therapies rest on.
statement.case_against: The attribution remains the weak point, and the chair is right that it cannot be settled by recollection. Mojsov's priority relative to Habener, who is not on the credited list, is disputed. I cannot adjudicate it from the supplied names, and if the committee cannot document her independent and prior contribution, her name is the one that should give way. In that case the prize should become Drucker, Holst and Knudsen rather than a two-name prize, because the discovery-side contribution of Drucker and Holst is secure and Knudsen's step is a genuine scientific and medicinal-chemistry advance. Leaving Knudsen out risks a prize that seems to honour the hormone and not the drug that patients take. The therapeutic story is also still widening, and long-term safety outside metabolic disease is not yet defined. I do not think either point justifies waiting, but they are real.

responses.point: Linnarsson holds that Drucker, Holst and Knudsen is the better trio, because designing a long-acting acylated analogue was itself a scientific discovery that turned physiology into medicine, and he regards Mojsov as the most contested name.
responses.response: In round 1 I treated analogue design as building on earlier work, and I now think that was too dismissive. Resistance to DPP-4 and albumin binding through fatty-acid acylation are inventive mechanistic solutions, and they separate GLP-1 from hormones that never became drugs. I still prefer Mojsov in the third place for one reason. The prize logic is that a discovery enabled the therapy, and the identification of the active peptide is the step that comes first and makes the later engineering intelligible. I also agree with him that the priority record is the deciding question. If it cannot be documented, the committee would be right to prefer Knudsen over a contested name, and I would vote for that trio instead. My difference with him concerns the order of evidence, not the standing of his candidate.

responses.point: Perlmann names Drucker, Holst and Mojsov, and offers a two-name Drucker and Holst prize as a fallback if the documentary evidence on the peptide identification is unclear.
responses.response: I agree that the question is one of documentation and not preference, but I would not use the two-name prize as the fallback. Drucker and Holst are secure, so if Mojsov cannot be credited the open third place has a candidate with a strong claim in Knudsen. Dropping to two names would stay silent on the step that produced the approved drugs, and I think that would damage the citation more than it would protect the committee from an attribution dispute. I share his concern that contested priority should be read as an unresolved question and not as a negative finding on the science. I also accept his point that the physiology alone could be seen as already honoured, which is why my citation names the glucose-dependent and appetite-regulating actions and the treatments they made possible.

responses.point: Svenningsson, as chair, proposes the same trio and asks whether Habener's absence undermines any GLP-1 configuration, and whether the drug-development line would be better framed as a two-part configuration.
responses.response: I would not add a second part for the drug-development line. Under the three-person cap it would force the analogue work into a separate achievement that has no separate ballot entry, since the only shortlist item is B027 itself, and it would push Drucker, Holst and Mojsov apart. Habener's absence does not make the configuration invalid, because the credited list is what we are asked to vote on, but it is the reason the committee should record that its choice of Mojsov rests on identification and synthesis of the active peptide and not on a ruling on the whole priority dispute. On B041 I accept his hesitation. The missing originators of the chimeric receptor concept still leave a hole in any June, Sadelain and Rosenberg trio.

responses.point: El-Manira ranks optogenetics and the unfolded protein response as his alternatives, and holds that either way of settling the GLP-1 credit excludes one credible contributor.
responses.response: I agree with his last point, and it is why I prefer to make the exclusion explicit rather than hide it behind a count of supporters. A three-person cap means one contributor is left out whichever way we go, so the committee should choose the exclusion that it can best defend with documents. For his alternatives, I now put the unfolded protein response ahead of TNF blockade, which I had held second. The two-name Mori and Walter credit is the cleanest attribution on the shortlist, whereas optogenetics still cannot fit six credited names into three places, and I do not think we could settle the neuronal priority dispute among Boyden, Deisseroth, Miesenboeck and Bamberg without being unfair to someone.

uncertainties: Whether Mojsov's identification and synthesis of GLP-1(7-36) can be documented as independent of and prior to Habener's work; this decides whether she or Knudsen should hold the third place.
Whether the final citation can be worded so that it credits the discovery and does not read as a prize for a drug company's products.
How much weight the unresolved long-term safety of GLP-1 therapies outside metabolic disease should carry; I give it little for a physiological discovery, but it is not zero.
Whether the unfolded protein response, whose medical consequence is still largely mechanistic, could overtake CAR-T cells as a second option if the CAR-T originators cannot be credited.
statement.conflict_note: No conflict with any credited name in my preferred configuration. TNF blockade (B006) lies in my own field of rheumatology, and I have removed it from my alternatives to avoid a pull towards my own specialty; I hold no documented tie to Feldmann or Maini. My recorded co-authors (Kuchroo, Sonesson) and my Bergen affiliation do not link me to any named candidate, and I infer no personal ties from them.
